title: World History
description: Free World History study guide from the first civilizations to the World Wars: river valleys, Greece and Rome, post-classical Asia and Africa, medieval Europe, the Renaissance, exploration, revolutions and the industrial age. 80 practice questions with explanations, 48 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Ancient Civilizations

concepts.intro: Farming changed how people lived more than almost any other development in history.
b: Around 10,000 BCE people in the Fertile Crescent began domesticating plants (wheat, barley) and animals
Agriculture produced food surpluses, which supported permanent villages and larger populations
Surpluses allowed specialization of labor: artisans, priests, soldiers and rulers
Farming arose independently in several places, including China, Mesoamerica and the Andes
Costs included more disease, social hierarchy and dependence on a few crops

concepts.intro: The first civilizations grew along rivers that provided water, fertile soil and transportation.
b: Mesopotamia (Tigris and Euphrates): Sumerian city-states, cuneiform writing, ziggurats
Egypt (Nile): pharaohs ruled as god-kings; hieroglyphics; pyramids built for the afterlife
Indus Valley: planned cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro with drainage systems; script still undeciphered
China (Yellow River / Huang He): Shang dynasty oracle bones; the Zhou claimed the Mandate of Heaven
Common features of civilization: cities, organized government, complex religion, specialization, social classes, writing

concepts.intro: Early states created lasting tools for organizing society.
b: Hammurabi's Code (Babylon, c. 1754 BCE) was one of the earliest written law codes: 'an eye for an eye'
Writing began as record-keeping for trade and taxes
Most early religions were polytheistic; the Hebrews developed monotheism
The Phoenicians spread an alphabet through Mediterranean trade
Bronze and later iron tools changed farming and warfare

keyFacts: The Neolithic Revolution began around 10,000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent.
Hammurabi's Code is one of the earliest written law codes.
Mandate of Heaven: Chinese belief that heaven grants and withdraws the right to rule.
Cuneiform (Mesopotamia) and hieroglyphics (Egypt) are early writing systems.
traps: Don't confuse the Tigris/Euphrates (Mesopotamia) with the Nile (Egypt) or the Huang He (China).
The Indus script hasn't been deciphered, so much about that society is inferred from archaeology.
Hammurabi's Code applied different punishments by social class. It wasn't 'equal justice'.

units.name: Classical Greece & Rome

concepts.intro: Greece was a collection of independent city-states (poleis) rather than one country.
b: Athens developed direct democracy under reformers like Cleisthenes and Pericles, though women, slaves and foreigners couldn't vote
Sparta was a militaristic oligarchy that trained boys as soldiers from age seven
Greek city-states united to defeat Persia in the Persian Wars (490–479 BCE)
The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta weakened Greece
Alexander the Great (d. 323 BCE) spread Greek culture across a huge empire: Hellenistic culture

concepts.intro: Greek thinkers shaped philosophy, science and the arts for centuries.
b: Socrates taught by questioning (the Socratic method)
Plato wrote The Republic and founded the Academy; Aristotle studied logic, science and politics
Greek drama, the Olympic Games and columned architecture (Parthenon) remain influential
Herodotus and Thucydides began writing history based on inquiry
Hellenistic scholars like Euclid and Archimedes advanced math and science

concepts.intro: Rome grew from a republic with elected officials into a vast empire.
b: The Roman Republic (509 BCE) had consuls, a Senate and, later, tribunes for plebeians
The Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE) put Roman law in writing
Julius Caesar's rise and assassination (44 BCE) ended the Republic; Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE
The Pax Romana (c. 27 BCE–180 CE) was two centuries of relative peace and trade
Christianity spread through the empire and was legalized by Constantine (313 CE); the Western Empire fell in 476 CE

keyFacts: Athens: direct democracy for adult male citizens.
Augustus became Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE.
Pax Romana: about 200 years of relative peace.
The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453.
traps: Athenian democracy excluded women, slaves and foreigners. It wasn't universal.
The Roman Republic wasn't a democracy in the modern sense; the Senate was dominated by patricians.
Rome didn't 'fall' all at once, and the Eastern Empire survived nearly a thousand more years.

units.name: Post-Classical Asia & Africa

concepts.intro: Islam spread rapidly after the 7th century, creating a vast network of trade and learning.
b: Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610 CE; the hijra to Medina in 622 marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar
The Five Pillars: faith, prayer, charity, fasting during Ramadan, and pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca
The Sunni–Shia split began over who should succeed Muhammad
The Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258) made Baghdad a center of learning (House of Wisdom)
Muslim scholars preserved Greek texts and advanced algebra, medicine and astronomy

concepts.intro: The Tang and Song dynasties were golden ages, followed by Mongol conquest.
b: The Tang (618–907) and Song (960–1279) expanded the civil service exam system based on Confucian learning
Song innovations: movable type, gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass, paper money
Genghis Khan united the Mongols (1206); his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history
Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China; Marco Polo described his court
The Pax Mongolica made Silk Road trade safer, but it also helped spread the Black Death

concepts.intro: Trade across the Sahara and Indian Ocean built wealthy African states.
b: Ghana, Mali and Songhai grew rich from the trans-Saharan gold–salt trade
Mansa Musa of Mali made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca (1324), displaying enormous wealth
Timbuktu became a center of Islamic scholarship
Swahili city-states on the East African coast traded in the Indian Ocean network
Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures reflect a wealthy inland trading state

keyFacts: 622 CE: the hijra, year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
Song China: movable type, compass, gunpowder weapons, paper money.
The Mongols built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Mali's wealth came from the gold–salt trade; Mansa Musa's hajj was in 1324.
traps: Gunpowder was invented in China, not Europe.
The Sunni–Shia split was about succession, not the Five Pillars.
African kingdoms like Mali were wealthy, literate trading states, not isolated from the wider world.

units.name: Medieval Europe

concepts.intro: After Rome's fall, Western Europe organized around land, loyalty and local protection.
b: Feudalism: lords granted land (fiefs) to vassals in exchange for military service and loyalty
Knights were mounted warriors bound by a code of chivalry
Manorialism: peasants and serfs worked a lord's manor in return for protection; serfs were bound to the land
Charlemagne was crowned emperor by the pope in 800 CE, reviving the idea of a western empire
Viking, Magyar and Muslim raids encouraged local defense and castles

concepts.intro: The Roman Catholic Church was the most powerful institution in medieval Western Europe.
b: The Church shaped daily life through sacraments, holidays and tithes
Monasteries preserved learning and copied manuscripts
Popes and kings clashed over authority, as in the Investiture Controversy
The Great Schism of 1054 split Christianity into Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox
The Crusades (1096–1291) were religious wars to control the Holy Land; they increased trade and contact with the Muslim world

concepts.l: Change in the Late Middle Ages
concepts.intro: Several shocks in the 1300s loosened the medieval order.
b: The Magna Carta (1215) limited the English king's power and protected nobles' rights
The Black Death (1347–1351) killed roughly a third of Europe's population
Labor shortages after the plague raised wages and weakened serfdom
The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France helped build national identity
Growing towns, guilds and trade fairs revived the economy

keyFacts: Feudalism: land for loyalty and military service.
Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800 CE.
Magna Carta (1215) limited the power of the English king.
The Black Death killed about one-third of Europe's population.
traps: Feudalism (lords and vassals) and manorialism (lords and peasants) aren't the same system.
The Crusades didn't permanently secure the Holy Land for Europeans.
The Magna Carta protected nobles first. It wasn't a democracy for everyone.

units.name: Renaissance & Reformation

concepts.intro: A 'rebirth' of interest in classical learning began in the Italian city-states around 1350.
b: Humanism focused on human potential and the study of classical Greek and Roman texts
Wealthy patrons like the Medici family of Florence funded artists and scholars
Artists used perspective and realism: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael
The Northern Renaissance (Erasmus, Dürer, Shakespeare) often blended humanism with Christian themes
Gutenberg's movable-type printing press (c. 1450) spread books and ideas quickly

concepts.intro: Criticism of Church practices split Western Christianity.
b: Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517, attacking the sale of indulgences
Luther taught salvation by faith alone and the authority of the Bible over Church tradition
John Calvin taught predestination and led a strict Protestant community in Geneva
Henry VIII broke with Rome and created the Church of England (1534), partly to annul his marriage
The printing press helped Protestant ideas spread rapidly

concepts.l: The Catholic Response and Its Effects
concepts.intro: The Catholic Church reformed itself while fighting Protestant expansion.
b: The Council of Trent (1545–1563) clarified Catholic doctrine and ended some abuses
The Jesuits (founded by Ignatius of Loyola) spread Catholic education and missions
Religious wars followed, including the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) strengthened the idea of sovereign states
The Reformation weakened papal authority and strengthened monarchs

keyFacts: Humanism: focus on human potential and classical learning.
Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1450) spread ideas fast.
Luther's 95 Theses: 1517.
Council of Trent: the core of the Catholic (Counter-) Reformation.
traps: The Renaissance began in Italy, not Northern Europe.
Luther didn't want to start a new church at first; he wanted to reform the Catholic Church.
Henry VIII's break with Rome was as much political and personal as doctrinal.

units.name: Age of Exploration

concepts.intro: European exploration was driven by 'God, gold and glory' and made possible by new technology.
b: Motives: spreading Christianity, finding wealth (spices, gold) and gaining national prestige
Europeans wanted a sea route to Asian spices that avoided Ottoman and Italian middlemen
Technology: the caravel, the magnetic compass, the astrolabe and better maps
Prince Henry of Portugal sponsored voyages down the African coast
Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around Africa (1498)

concepts.intro: Columbus's 1492 voyage began sustained contact between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
b: Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492
Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire (1521); Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca (1530s)
Diseases like smallpox killed a large majority of the Indigenous population, a catastrophic decline
The encomienda system forced Indigenous people to labor for Spanish colonists
The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal

concepts.l: The Columbian Exchange and Global Trade
concepts.intro: Plants, animals, people and diseases moved between hemispheres.
b: From the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco
From the Eastern Hemisphere to the Americas: horses, cattle, wheat, sugarcane and diseases
The Atlantic slave trade forcibly moved about 12 million Africans across the Atlantic
Mercantilism: nations sought wealth (gold, favorable trade) and used colonies as sources of raw materials
Silver from Potosí and Mexico flowed to Europe and China, linking a global economy

keyFacts: Motives: God, gold and glory.
1492: Columbus reaches the Caribbean.
Columbian Exchange: transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between hemispheres.
About 12 million Africans were forced across the Atlantic in the slave trade.
traps: Disease, not just warfare, caused most Indigenous deaths after contact.
Potatoes and maize went from the Americas to Europe, not the other way.
Columbus didn't prove the Earth was round; educated Europeans already knew that.

units.name: Revolutions & Enlightenment

concepts.intro: New methods of inquiry led thinkers to apply reason to society and government.
b: Copernicus proposed a sun-centered (heliocentric) model; Galileo supported it with telescope observations
Newton's laws of motion and gravity (1687) showed nature follows mathematical laws
John Locke: natural rights to life, liberty and property; government by consent of the governed
Montesquieu: separation of powers; Rousseau: the social contract and popular sovereignty
Voltaire championed freedom of speech and religion

concepts.intro: Enlightenment ideas inspired revolutions against monarchy.
b: The American Declaration of Independence (1776) echoed Locke's natural rights
The French Revolution began in 1789 amid debt, food shortages and inequality among the three estates
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) proclaimed liberty and equality
The Reign of Terror (1793–1794) under Robespierre executed thousands
Napoleon rose to power, spread revolutionary legal reforms (Napoleonic Code) and was defeated at Waterloo in 1815

concepts.intro: Enlightenment ideas and weakened European powers helped Latin American colonies win independence.
b: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), led by Toussaint Louverture, created the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people
Simón Bolívar led independence movements in northern South America
José de San Martín led independence in Argentina, Chile and Peru
Creoles (American-born people of European descent) often led these revolutions
Mexico's independence movement began with Father Hidalgo's call in 1810

keyFacts: Locke: natural rights of life, liberty and property.
Montesquieu: separation of powers.
French Revolution began in 1789.
Haiti (1804): first nation founded after a successful revolt of enslaved people.
traps: Locke, not Rousseau, is the source of 'life, liberty and property'.
The French Revolution didn't lead straight to democracy; it passed through the Terror and Napoleon.
Creoles, not peninsulares, led most Latin American independence movements.

units.name: Industrial Age & World Wars

concepts.intro: Machine production transformed economies and societies, starting in Britain in the late 1700s.
b: Britain had coal and iron, capital, colonies, a large labor force and stable government
Key inventions: the steam engine (improved by James Watt), the spinning jenny, the power loom
Factories moved work out of homes; cities grew rapidly (urbanization)
Harsh conditions (long hours, child labor, pollution) sparked labor unions and reforms
New ideas: capitalism (Adam Smith), socialism, and Marx and Engels' Communist Manifesto (1848)

concepts.intro: Industrial power fueled empires and, eventually, a world war.
b: Industrial nations sought raw materials and markets, leading to the Scramble for Africa (Berlin Conference, 1884–85)
Causes of WWI: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism (MAIN)
Spark: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (1914)
Trench warfare, machine guns and poison gas caused enormous casualties
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany, imposed reparations and redrew borders

concepts.intro: The Depression and resentment of Versailles helped bring totalitarian regimes and a second world war.
b: The Great Depression (from 1929) created economic desperation
Fascist and totalitarian leaders rose: Mussolini (Italy), Hitler (Germany); militarists in Japan
Appeasement failed; Germany's invasion of Poland (1939) started the war in Europe
The Holocaust: the Nazi genocide of about six million Jews and millions of others
The war ended in 1945; the United Nations was founded and the Cold War began

keyFacts: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s.
MAIN causes of WWI: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism.
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany and required reparations.
The Holocaust killed about six million Jews.
traps: Franz Ferdinand's assassination sparked WWI but wasn't its only cause.
Marx wrote The Communist Manifesto; Adam Smith defended free-market capitalism.
WWII in Europe began in 1939 with Poland, not with Pearl Harbor (1941).

quiz.q: What was the most important result of the Neolithic Revolution?
o: Food surpluses that supported permanent settlements
quiz.e: Farming produced surpluses, which made villages, specialization and eventually cities possible.

quiz.q: Mesopotamia developed between which two rivers?
quiz.e: 'Mesopotamia' means 'land between the rivers'.

quiz.q: Cuneiform was:
o: A wedge-shaped writing system from Mesopotamia
quiz.e: Scribes pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets.

quiz.q: Hammurabi's Code is significant because it:
o: Was one of the earliest written legal codes
quiz.e: Writing laws down made rules and punishments public, though they varied by class.

quiz.q: The Mandate of Heaven was used in China to:
o: Organize trade on the Silk Road
Establish Buddhism as the state religion
Justify a dynasty's rule and the overthrow of failing rulers
quiz.e: Disasters and unrest could be read as a loss of heaven's mandate, justifying a new dynasty.

quiz.q: Which feature did Harappa and Mohenjo-daro share?
o: Planned grid streets and drainage systems
quiz.e: Indus Valley cities are known for sophisticated urban planning.

quiz.q: Specialization of labor became possible mainly because of:
quiz.e: When not everyone needed to farm, people could take on other jobs.

quiz.q: Which group is credited with spreading an early alphabet across the Mediterranean?
quiz.e: Phoenician traders spread their alphabet, an ancestor of Greek and Latin letters.

quiz.q: Egyptian pharaohs were generally viewed as:
quiz.e: Pharaohs were seen as divine or semi-divine rulers.

quiz.q: The ancient Hebrews are most associated with:
quiz.e: Belief in one God distinguished the Hebrews from most neighbors.

quiz.q: Athenian democracy was 'direct' because:
quiz.e: Male citizens voted in the Assembly directly rather than through representatives.

quiz.q: Sparta is best known for its:
quiz.e: Spartan society centered on training soldiers.

quiz.q: Who spread Hellenistic culture from Greece to Egypt and India?
quiz.e: His conquests blended Greek and local cultures.

quiz.q: The Socratic method teaches through:
quiz.e: Socrates questioned students to expose assumptions.

quiz.q: The Twelve Tables were important because they:
quiz.e: Written law limited arbitrary decisions by officials.

quiz.q: Who became Rome's first emperor?
quiz.e: Octavian took the title Augustus in 27 BCE.

quiz.q: The Pax Romana was a period of:
quiz.e: About 200 years of stability helped trade and culture flourish.

quiz.q: Which war weakened the Greek city-states before Macedonian conquest?
quiz.e: Athens and Sparta fought each other from 431 to 404 BCE.

quiz.q: Constantine is significant for:
quiz.e: The Edict of Milan (313 CE) granted religious toleration.

quiz.q: In what year is the fall of the Western Roman Empire traditionally dated?
quiz.e: The last Western emperor was deposed in 476.

quiz.q: The hijra of 622 CE was:
o: Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina
quiz.e: It marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

quiz.q: Which is one of the Five Pillars of Islam?
quiz.e: The pillars are faith, prayer, charity, fasting and the hajj to Mecca.

quiz.q: The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims began over:
quiz.e: Shia Muslims believed leadership should pass through Ali's line.

quiz.q: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad was:
o: A center of translation and scholarship
quiz.e: Scholars translated and built on Greek, Persian and Indian works.

quiz.q: Which innovation came from Song dynasty China?
o: The printing press with metal type in Mainz
quiz.e: Bi Sheng developed movable type in the 11th century.

quiz.q: China's civil service exams tested candidates on:
quiz.e: Officials were chosen, in principle, by merit in Confucian learning.

quiz.q: The Pax Mongolica helped:
o: End contact between Europe and Asia
Trade flourish along the Silk Road
quiz.e: Mongol control made long-distance travel safer.

quiz.q: Mali's wealth came mainly from:
o: The trans-Saharan gold and salt trade
quiz.e: Mali controlled gold fields and trade routes.

quiz.q: Mansa Musa is famous for:
quiz.e: His 1324 hajj displayed Mali's wealth across North Africa.

quiz.q: Swahili city-states such as Kilwa were part of which trade network?
quiz.e: East African ports traded with Arabia, Persia, India and China.

quiz.q: Under feudalism, a vassal received land in exchange for:
quiz.e: Fiefs were granted for service, especially military service.

quiz.q: Serfs were:
o: Peasants bound to the land they worked
quiz.e: Serfs couldn't leave the manor without the lord's permission.

quiz.q: Charlemagne was crowned emperor by the pope in:
quiz.e: The coronation revived the idea of a Roman-style empire in the West.

quiz.q: The Great Schism of 1054 divided:
o: Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christianity
quiz.e: Disputes over authority and practice split the Church.

quiz.q: One major effect of the Crusades was:
o: A permanent European kingdom in Jerusalem
Increased trade and contact between Europe and the Middle East
quiz.e: Crusaders brought back goods and ideas, stimulating trade.

quiz.q: The Magna Carta (1215) is significant because it:
o: Created the English Parliament's House of Commons
Limited the king's power under the law
quiz.e: It established that the king wasn't above the law.

quiz.q: About what share of Europe's population died in the Black Death?
quiz.e: Estimates range from 30 to 50% in many regions.

quiz.q: How did the Black Death weaken serfdom?
o: Labor shortages let surviving workers demand better wages
Kings freed serfs as a reward
quiz.e: With fewer workers, peasants gained bargaining power.

quiz.q: Monasteries were important in medieval Europe because they:
quiz.e: Monks copied classical and religious texts.

quiz.q: The Hundred Years' War was fought between:
o: The pope and the Holy Roman Emperor
quiz.e: It lasted from 1337 to 1453, with Joan of Arc a famous figure.

quiz.q: Renaissance humanism emphasized:
o: Rejecting all Greek and Roman texts
quiz.e: Humanists studied classical texts and celebrated human achievement.

quiz.q: Where did the Renaissance begin?
quiz.e: Wealthy Italian cities like Florence and Venice funded the arts.

quiz.q: The Medici family were important as:
o: Patrons of the arts in Florence
quiz.e: Their banking wealth funded artists and scholars.

quiz.q: Which invention most helped Reformation ideas spread?
quiz.e: Pamphlets and Bibles could be printed quickly and cheaply.

quiz.q: Martin Luther's 95 Theses (1517) criticized:
quiz.e: Luther objected to selling forgiveness of sins.

quiz.q: Luther taught that salvation comes through:
quiz.e: Sola fide, faith alone, was central to his theology.

quiz.q: John Calvin is most associated with:
quiz.e: Calvin taught that God had already chosen who would be saved.

quiz.q: Why did Henry VIII break with the Catholic Church?
o: The pope refused to annul his marriage
quiz.e: The Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king head of the Church of England.

quiz.q: The Council of Trent was part of the:
quiz.e: It clarified Catholic doctrine and reformed abuses.

quiz.q: The Jesuits were founded to:
quiz.e: They were leaders of the Catholic response to Protestantism.

quiz.q: 'God, gold and glory' summarizes:
quiz.e: Religion, wealth and prestige drove exploration.

quiz.q: Which technology helped sailors determine latitude?
quiz.e: The astrolabe measured the angle of the sun or stars above the horizon.

quiz.q: Vasco da Gama was the first European to:
o: Reach India by sailing around Africa
quiz.e: His 1498 voyage opened a sea route to Asia.

quiz.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided lands between:
quiz.e: A papal-brokered line split new claims between the two powers.

quiz.q: What was the main cause of Indigenous population decline in the Americas after 1492?
quiz.e: Indigenous peoples had no immunity to Eurasian diseases.

quiz.q: Who conquered the Aztec Empire?
quiz.e: Cortés and his Indigenous allies took Tenochtitlan in 1521.

quiz.q: Which crop traveled from the Americas to Europe in the Columbian Exchange?
quiz.e: Potatoes became a staple crop in Europe.

quiz.q: Which animal was introduced to the Americas by Europeans?
quiz.e: Horses transformed life on the Great Plains.

quiz.q: Mercantilism held that a nation's power depended on:
o: Accumulating wealth and a favorable balance of trade
quiz.e: Colonies supplied raw materials and bought finished goods.

quiz.q: The encomienda system:
o: Forced Indigenous people to work for Spanish colonists
Divided the world between Spain and Portugal
quiz.e: It was a system of coerced labor.

quiz.q: Who proposed a heliocentric (sun-centered) model of the universe?
quiz.e: Galileo later supported it with observations.

quiz.q: John Locke argued that people have natural rights to:
quiz.e: Governments exist to protect these rights, by the consent of the governed.

quiz.q: Montesquieu is best known for proposing:
quiz.e: He argued power should be divided among branches.

quiz.q: Which document most directly reflects Locke's ideas?
quiz.e: It speaks of unalienable rights and consent of the governed.

quiz.q: A major cause of the French Revolution was:
o: The end of the slave trade
Heavy debt and unequal taxation of the Third Estate
quiz.e: The Third Estate paid most taxes while the clergy and nobles were largely exempt.

quiz.q: The Reign of Terror was led by:
quiz.e: The Committee of Public Safety executed suspected enemies of the Revolution.

quiz.q: The Napoleonic Code:
o: Created a uniform set of laws in France
quiz.e: It spread ideas like legal equality for men across Europe.

quiz.q: The Haitian Revolution is unique because it:
o: Was led by the French king
Created a nation led by formerly enslaved people
quiz.e: Haiti became independent in 1804.

quiz.q: Simón Bolívar is known as:
o: A liberator of northern South America
The leader of the Haitian Revolution
quiz.e: He led independence for present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia.

quiz.q: Napoleon's final defeat came at:
quiz.e: He was then exiled to Saint Helena.

quiz.q: Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain?
o: It had coal, iron, capital and a stable government
It had the largest population in the world
quiz.e: Resources, capital and markets gave Britain an early lead.

quiz.q: Who improved the steam engine to make it practical for industry?
quiz.e: Watt's improvements (1760s–1780s) made steam power efficient.

quiz.q: Urbanization during the Industrial Revolution means:
o: People moved to cities for factory work
quiz.e: Factory jobs drew workers into growing cities.

quiz.q: The Communist Manifesto (1848) was written by:
quiz.e: It called for workers to overthrow capitalism.

quiz.q: The Berlin Conference (1884–85) is associated with:
quiz.e: European powers set rules for claiming African territory.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the MAIN causes of World War I?
quiz.e: MAIN stands for militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism.

quiz.q: The immediate spark of World War I was:
o: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
quiz.e: He was killed in Sarajevo in June 1914.

quiz.q: The Treaty of Versailles:
quiz.e: Its harsh terms bred resentment in Germany.

quiz.q: What event began World War II in Europe?
quiz.e: Britain and France declared war two days later.

quiz.q: The Holocaust was:
o: A battle on the Eastern Front
The Nazi genocide of about six million Jews and millions of others
quiz.e: It was a systematic, state-organized mass murder.

PART_B2.q: Explain two ways the Neolithic Revolution changed human societies.
PART_B2.sa: Strong answers name two specific changes and explain them. Food surpluses from farming let people settle permanently and populations grow. Surpluses also let some people specialize (artisans, priests, rulers), which led to social classes, government and eventually cities. Other valid points: new technologies such as pottery and plows, and environmental change.

PART_B2.q: Compare the goals of the Protestant Reformation and the Catholic Reformation.
PART_B2.sa: Both responded to problems in the Church. Protestants such as Luther and Calvin rejected papal authority, taught salvation by faith and put scripture over tradition, and many broke away to form new churches. The Catholic Reformation kept papal authority and traditional doctrine (Council of Trent) while ending abuses such as selling indulgences and spreading the faith through the Jesuits.

PART_C.q: To what extent were the American, French and Haitian revolutions shaped by Enlightenment ideas? Use specific evidence from at least two revolutions.
PART_C.sa: A strong essay takes a clear position and supports it with evidence. Enlightenment influence: the Declaration of Independence uses Locke's natural rights and consent of the governed; the French Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaims liberty, equality and popular sovereignty (Rousseau). Haitian revolutionaries used 'liberty and equality' to demand the end of slavery. Limits: economic causes (French debt and bread prices), local grievances (taxation without representation) and the brutal slave system in Saint-Domingue also drove events, and none of the revolutions immediately granted rights to everyone (women, enslaved people in the U.S.).

PART_C.q: Explain how industrialization contributed to both imperialism and World War I.
PART_C.sa: Industrial economies needed raw materials (rubber, cotton, oil) and new markets, which drove European imperial expansion such as the Scramble for Africa. Industrial power also built modern militaries and arms races (militarism), and competition for colonies deepened rivalries and alliances. Industrial weapons (machine guns, artillery, gas) and mass mobilization made WWI unusually deadly once it began in 1914.
